terms.notes: `programu` also serves as the noun for "program/software"; use `kupanga programu` for the activity of programming. Medium confidence; institutional sources disagree on a single preferred verb form.
Well attested across dictionary and community sources.
Compositional (`sekta` = sector, `teknolojia` = nativized loanword "technology"); not independently sourced as a fixed phrase but low ambiguity risk.
Ordinary word for "a series/succession, in a row"; not CS-specific but a natural fit for a daily-use streak.
Ordinary word ("trap"); natural extension.
Ordinary word; medium confidence, sourced from Kilinux terminology project.
Very well established across all sources. `nambari` is an accepted variant.
Compositional (`kamili` = whole/complete); confirmed in math-education Swahili, extended to CS by analogy. Medium confidence.
Nativized loanword; confirmed only in math-education sources, not CS-specific. Medium confidence.
Ordinary word for "letter/character". Medium confidence.
Low-medium confidence: sourced from two independent hobbyist Swahili-keyword programming languages (Nuru, Jenga on GitHub), not an institutional source. Flag for native-speaker review.
Ordinary word for "list". Medium confidence.

No credible CS-specific source found, and real risk of collision with `kamusi` (a literal dictionary/reference book). Give the gloss "kama kamusi, inaunganisha funguo na thamani" (like a dictionary, links keys to values) where the source `<define>`s it. Open question for native-speaker review.
Sourced from a Swahili Wikipedia OOP article. Medium confidence. Note: reserved for the data-structure sense; platform "feature" uses a different word (`huduma`) to avoid collision.
No credible source found. Gloss as "nafasi ya kipengele katika orodha" (the position of an element in a list) where the source `<define>`s it. Low confidence / open question.

No credible CS-specific source found; `mfuatano` ("sequence") surfaced only as an unconfirmed candidate. Gloss as "mfuatano wa herufi" (a sequence of characters) where the source `<define>`s it, then use `string`.
Gloss as "aina ya data yenye thamani mbili tu: kweli au sikweli" (a data type with only two values: true or false) where the source `<define>`s it, then use `Boolean`.
Compositional, sourced from a Swahili Wikipedia Python article. Medium confidence.
Compositional (`kauli` = statement, `masharti` = conditions). The `if` keyword itself always stays English in code, per global rules. Low-medium confidence, not directly sourced.
Ordinary word.
Ordinary word, from the verb `kulinganisha` (to compare). Extrapolated, not CS-source-confirmed, but low ambiguity risk.
Ordinary word ("utterance/expression"). Extrapolated.

Candidates (`mwendeshaji`, `kiendeshi`) found only in low-confidence crowd dictionaries. Gloss as "kiendeshi, k.m. `+`, `-`" (an operator, e.g. `+`, `-`) where the source `<define>`s it, then use `operator`.

The imperative sense: a line of code that does something and gets executed. Chosen distinct from `kauli` (below) to avoid the collision `global/terms.md` flags between the two senses of "statement". Low-medium confidence.
The proposition sense: a claim that is true or false. Ordinary word.

Also the ordinary word for "work/job"; always clarify where the source `<define>`s it to avoid ambiguity. The `function` keyword in code stays English; the concept in prose is `kazi`. Medium confidence, sourced from a Swahili Wikipedia Python article.
Ordinary verb ("to call/summon"), natural extension: `kuita kazi` = to call a function.
"To create/construct". Low confidence, not directly sourced.

The candidate `kigezo` is contested (also used loosely for "criterion" and, unresolved, for "variable"). Gloss as "jina la thamani inayotarajiwa na kazi" (the name of the value a function expects) where the source `<define>`s it, then use `parameter`.

No credible source found; kept distinct from `parameter` per `global/terms.md`. Gloss as "thamani halisi inayotolewa wakati wa kuita kazi" (the actual value given when calling a function) where the source `<define>`s it.
Native coinage from `kuingiza` (to insert). Medium confidence, sourced from a UDSM thesis (Malagira 2010).
Ordinary word ("results/outcomes"). Low-medium confidence.
Ordinary, transparent verb ("to return/give back").
Compositional ("the value that is returned"), kept distinct from the verb above. Low confidence, but transparent.
No credible source found. Gloss as "neno muhimu la lugha ya programu" (an important word of the programming language) where the source `<define>`s it.

The single biggest gap found in research: the candidate `kigezo` appears only in math-education sources and also ordinarily means "criterion", causing real ambiguity risk. Gloss as "kigezo" where the source `<define>`s it with the explanation "mahali panapohifadhi thamani" (a place that stores a value), then use `variable`. Flag for native-speaker review; this may become a settled Swahili term once confirmed.

Risk of collision with `kugawa` ("to divide/allocate"). Gloss as "kuweka thamani kwenye variable" (to put a value into a variable) where the source `<define>`s it, then use `assignment` / `to assign`.
Compositional (`msimbo` = code, sourced medium confidence; `kizuizi` = block/barrier). Low-medium confidence, not directly sourced as a fixed phrase.
Well attested across multiple sources. `kosa` is an accepted variant.
Use "uliowekwa ndani ya" (placed inside), e.g. `kitanzi kilichowekwa ndani ya kitanzi kingine` = nested loop. No single-word coinage confirmed; a descriptive phrase is more reliable than forcing one.
From `kurudia` (to repeat). Low-medium confidence, not CS-source-confirmed.
Ordinary verb ("to run/drive"). Extrapolated but low ambiguity risk.
Low-medium confidence: converges across three independent crowd dictionaries, but no institutional source confirmed it as the CS term. Flag for native-speaker review.
Keep `for` in backticks (real keyword) + `kitanzi`.
As above, with `while`.
Compositional ("body of the loop"). Low confidence, transparent.
Gloss as "wigo" (range/scope, ordinary word) where the source `<define>`s it, then use `scope`. Mirrors the "keep English" treatment other languages give this term.
Ordinarily means "classroom/school class"; always clarify where the source `<define>`s it to avoid ambiguity. Medium confidence, sourced from a Swahili Wikipedia Python article.
Nativized loanword, transparently recognizable; no clarification needed. Medium confidence.
Ordinarily means "quality/attribute/praise"; clarify where the source `<define>`s it. Medium confidence.

Two independent Swahili Wikipedia CS articles give conflicting terms (`kiumbile` vs `mfano`), a bad sign for confidence in this cluster. Gloss as "kitu" (thing, generic) where the source `<define>`s it, then use `object`. Flag for native-speaker review.
Compositional ("flow of work"). Low-medium confidence, not directly sourced.

Research pattern (SUMAIT 2022 paper) shows newer/web-era terms like this are commonly left bare in real Swahili tech usage. Gloss as "kuweka programu tayari kutumika" (to put a program ready for use) where the source `<define>`s it, then use `deploy`.
Ordinary word ("tool/instrument"), extrapolated but low ambiguity risk.
Nativized loanword, pattern-consistent with `metodu`/`akaunti`/`adapta`, but not independently confirmed for this specific term. Low confidence.
Also ordinarily means "rule/law/principle"; always clarify where the source `<define>`s it to avoid ambiguity. Medium confidence.

Research found conflicting coinages (a heavy native-coinage version on Swahili Wikipedia vs a looser, likely machine-translated paraphrase elsewhere). Explain the concept in Swahili where the source `<define>`s it rather than just glossing the acronym, per `global/rules.md`: "njia ambayo programu mbili zinawasiliana" (a way two programs communicate with each other), then use `API`.
The candidate `mfumo` is generic ("system/structure") with real ambiguity risk. Gloss as "mfumo" where the source `<define>`s it, then use `framework`.

Only weakly sourced (`kiolesura cha amri`, single source). Explain the concept where the source `<define>`s it: "njia ya kutumia kompyuta kwa kuandika amri" (a way of using a computer by typing commands), then use `CLI`.
Gloss as "sehemu" (part/component, ordinary word) where the source `<define>`s it, then use `component`.
